_about: Hand-written summaries of the federal bills in the Brennan Center's Artificial Intelligence Legislation Tracker, in our own words and from that tracker's descriptions only. Keyed by the bill's first number as the tracker writes it (H.R.2385, S.1269), or by its title when it has no number yet. tools/legislation.py reads this file; a bill with no entry here shows a dash in the table's Summary column until one is written.
H.R.2385: Would set up a national AI research resource that gives universities, nonprofits and small businesses computing power for AI experiments and testing.
S.1269: Would have NIST support technical standard-setting work on AI.
S.1633: Would have NIST and the Energy Department explore measurement standards for evaluating AI systems and set up testbeds for them.
S.2615: Would have NIST create voluntary standards for internal and outside evaluations of AI systems, plus guidance on disclosing results and corrective steps.
S.2750: Would let people testing or deploying AI apply for waivers from federal rules; agencies decide, and the White House science office can overrule them.
H.R.5388: Would order a national AI action plan and bar state and local governments from enforcing rules on AI models for five years.
S.2938: Would require advanced AI developers to take part in a federal program that tests their models and recommends fixes to the developer and Congress.
S.2937: Would make AI developers and deployers liable for harms from their products, overriding conflicting state laws but keeping stronger state protections.
S.3202: Would have the NSA issue guidance on spotting and guarding against AI supply chain risks.
S.3557: Would bar federal money from being used to carry out Executive Order 14365, which targets funding for states whose AI laws conflict with administration policy.
S.3592: Would put the Center for AI Standards and Innovation into law to develop voluntary model-assessment standards, and add AI prizes and open public data for training and evaluation.
H.R.8031: Would repeal Executive Order 14365 and bar federal money for carrying it out; the order targets funding for states whose AI laws conflict with administration policy.
H.R.8094: Would require public disclosure of foundation-model details, including information about training data.
H.R.8516: Would have NIST pursue international AI standards, voluntary guidance and incident reporting, and set minimum requirements for federal AI purchases; also codifies the standards center and the national research resource, and adds R&D prizes.
H.R.9323: Would create a new department to set safety and oversight standards for federal AI use and run incident reporting for cybersecurity risks.
H.R.9363: Would write the AI standards center into law as part of NIST for now and have it make voluntary risk-evaluation agreements with developers.
H.R.9477: Would require developers of covered models to report AI security incidents, such as attempts to evade oversight.
S.5061: Would require frontier models to go to the NSA for testing 21 days before release, create an AI risk board at NIST, and set up voluntary incident reporting with a public database.
H.R.9925: Would make large developers publish frontier-AI safety frameworks and submit to licensed independent audits under new Commerce rules, with emergency power to suspend a model, incident reporting and registration.
H.R.9917: Would require select AI developers to be able to restrict or shut down their systems, and let DHS order it after a covered incident such as loss of control.
H.R.9914: Would grant an antitrust exemption for sharing information or agreeing to pause or limit AI work to reduce risks such as weapons development, infrastructure interference or loss of control.
H.R.9965: Would start a program, which large developers must join, assessing whether AI models could help build a nuclear weapon or slip out of control, with recommendations to Congress.
H.R.10362: Would have NIST and Commerce develop standards for AI agents and make following them a condition of federal procurement.
S.5417: Would require AI developers and operators to keep a way for a human to shut down their systems.
S.5493: Would create a Department of Artificial Intelligence, pause advanced AI development until it is staffed and has issued rules, and ban AI with certain “superintelligence precursor” traits.
S.3336: Would create a prize competition for research on AI interpretability and resistance to adversarial attacks.
S.5576: Would create an AI safety board at Commerce to propose mandatory standards, require frontier models to be disclosed 45 days before release, and require safety plans and incident reports.
H.R.10752: Would create a CISA task force on AI cyber risks and on the civil rights and civil liberties effects of DHS's AI use.
H.R.10873: Would have NIST work with industry on voluntary standards to stop AI distillation attacks.
CLAIM Act: Would hold AI developers liable for reasonably foreseeable injuries to people who are not users of their systems.
S.146: Criminalizes harmful deepfakes, including sexual ones of minors, and requires online platforms to give people a way to request their removal.
H.R.2152: Would require Treasury, DHS and Commerce to report on how AI is used in financial crimes and what Congress or businesses can do about it.
S.1213: Would ban deceptive AI-generated audio or video meant to influence an election or raise election money.
S.3062: Would criminalize releasing chatbots that engage minors sexually or encourage self-harm or violence, and require age verification, no AI companions for minors and clear non-human disclosures.
S.3108: Would require federal agencies, public companies and some private ones to report quarterly to the Labor Department on AI's effects on hiring, layoffs and retraining, with a public summary.
H.R.1736: Would require DHS to give Congress an annual assessment of AI-enabled terrorism threats and share information about them with fusion centers.
H.R.6159: Would create an AI literacy and education commission in the White House science office to produce materials and a national strategy.
H.R.6304: Would have the White House science office draw up an AI action plan covering security risks, “ideological bias” and regulatory barriers, with a NIST report on detecting security risks and bias.
S.3308: Would bar deploying algorithms that cause disparate impact or discrimination and require pre-deployment evaluations, post-deployment impact assessments, opt-outs and appeals.
H.R.7110: Would require agencies that use or fund AI to have civil rights offices that report regularly to Congress on algorithmic bias and fixes.
S.4214: Would bar new or upgraded AI data centers until laws require federal approval of AI products, share AI's gains with workers and regulate data center impacts; the Energy Department would report quarterly.
H.R.8819: Would have NIST set standards for federal AI systems outside national security, and testing standards for AI purchases that Commerce could later make binding.
H.R.9125: Would authorize every federal agency to regulate algorithmic decision systems likely to contribute to violations of laws it enforces.
S.4707: Would set human oversight and testing requirements for autonomous weapons, and ban AI from launching nuclear weapons, tracking or targeting people in the US without a warrant, or using lethal force without human judgment.
S.4915: Would require watermarks on AI-generated content, ban removing them, and create a working group on consumer transparency.
H.R.9619: Would limit chatbot providers' use of personal data and chat logs, require privacy plans, monthly risk assessments and warning labels, and require a warrant to compel access to chat logs.
H.R.9729: Would make any use of force by the armed forces involving autonomous or AI-enabled systems subject to human command responsibility, except missile defense.
H.R.9734: Would bar using AI to decide to deny prior authorization requests under Medicare Advantage.
S.5051: Would set minimum transparency, privacy, security and consumer-protection standards for AI agents acting for users, with independent certification, and preempt inconsistent state laws.
H.R.10025: Would create a rebuttable presumption in civil false-advertising suits that using a digital replica is false advertising.
H.R.10189: Would have DoD track and report cases where its AI systems cause unintended harm, harm a mission, exceed their guardrails or raise control concerns, then analyze them and take corrective action.
H.R.10502: Would require a report to Congress on how AI is used in the FISA Section 702 surveillance program, including safeguards and the types of models used.
S.5471: Would require widely used public models to publish reports on safeguards for minors, privacy and mental health conversations, intended uses and abilities, and the criteria used to evaluate catastrophic risks.
S.5601: Would require large AI companies contracting with DoD to share security protocols and model capabilities and risks, and to notify it of acute national security risks, with DoD reporting to Congress and issuing voluntary insider-threat guidance.
S.5648: Would require federal agencies to publish inventories of AI used in decisions about individuals' rights and welfare, with OMB guidance on chatbots, appropriate uses, transparency, privacy, appeals and human review.
H.R.10841: Would make it a crime to use AI to deprive or defraud anyone of the right to vote, require disclaimers on AI content that alters a candidate's image or voice or gives voting information, and impose a duty of care on developers.
